newsitem.title: INDIA: India praises Deng for ties but expects no change.
newsitem.headline: India praises Deng for ties but expects no change.

text.p: India on Thursday mourned the death of Chinese patriarch Deng Xiaoping, saying he was largely responsible for improving ties between the two Asian giants.
But analysts said they did not expect any dramatic improvement in relations after Deng's passing.

"We express our heartfelt grief at the death of the great personality," Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral told Reuters. "He not only shaped the destiny of his nation but contributed directly to building good relations between our two countries."

Deng, whose pragmatic market reforms propelled China on to the world stage as an emerging economic superpower, was in the advanced stages of Parkinson's disease. He died of respiratory failure at 9.08 p.m. (1308 GMT) on Wednesday in Beijing, the official Xinhua news agency said.
The then prime minister Rajiv Gandhi visited Beijing in 1988 and met Deng, ending years of suspicion following a brief border war in 1962.
"That was a historic moment which determined the course of our future relations," Gujral said.
Analysts polled by Reuters said ties between the giant neighbours had not made much headway on the issue of the 4,056 km (2,535 mile) border straddling their Himalayan frontiers.
China claims some 90,000 sq km (35,000 sq miles) in India's northeastern Arunachal Pradesh. China also regards India's northern Sikkim state as disputed.
India says China occupies about 33,000 sq km (13,000 sq miles) in the Aksai Chin region of its northern Jammu and Kashmir state.
"I have not seen a qualitative movement forward on the boundary question since 1993," former Indian foreign secretary Jyotindra Nath Dixit told Reuters.

Dixit was the top civil servant in the foreign ministry when then prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao signed a landmark treaty of "peace and tranquillity" along the India-China border with Premier Li Peng in Beijing.
Chinese President Jiang Zemin, Deng's anointed successor, visited India last year.
"Jiang's visit was a great boost to the continuing process of peace and reconciliation," Gujral said. "His presence as a key player will naturally help our ties."
Defence anlayst Jasjit Singh said Deng's death was not likely to affect India's security concerns about China.
"While changes in leadership will always remain an issue, Deng was not effective for a long time," Singh, director of the state-funded Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses said.
"Of course, Deng's policy of better relations with neighbours meant better relations with India. But only coming decades will show us how it is translated into a substantive reality," Singh said.
India's relations with China have frequently soured over the refuge New Delhi has given to the Dalai Lama, Tibet's spiritual leader, who fled to India after a failed anti-Chinese uprising in 1959.

Singh said while India's relations with the Dalai Lama had been subdued recently, his presence at the head of a government-in-exile in the Himalayan Indian town of Dharamsala would continue to rankle the Chinese.
The Dalai Lama issued a statement regretting that Deng had not been able to resolve the dispute over Tibet.

"Deng Xiaoping had been involved in the Tibetan issue from the very beginning, all the way through right up to the end, so it seems he had the intention to resolve the Tibetan issue himself during this own lifetime," the Dalai Lama said in an interview with the Tibetan service of Voice of America radio.
"Perhaps he regretted this; for me, even now I cannot find a way to resolve it, so I regret that," the Dalai Lama said.
